tasks.title: Restore limit enforcement in proxyauth file generation
tasks.description: Ensure that the live user file (/etc/3proxy/users/.proxyauth) carries the d<bytes>, e<timestamp>, and i<count> flags alongside the CR hash. Decide the source of truth for each flag (dataLimit in MB -> bytes, expiresAt -> unix seconds, ipLimit) and emit them in proxyauthEntry(). tasks.details: Modify proxyauthEntry() in the config generation logic to include limit flags. Map dataLimit (MB) to bytes for d<bytes>, expiresAt (ISO) to unix seconds for e<timestamp>, and ipLimit to i<count>. Remove the write to /etc/3proxy-users.cfg in api/config/generate POST. tasks.testStrategy: Run a container and verify .proxyauth contains the flags. Restart 3proxy and confirm a user over their data limit is cut off. Confirm a deactivated user is rejected. Verify 3proxy accepts quoted CR hashes in included files.

subtasks.title: Map ProxyUser fields to 3proxy flag syntax
subtasks.description:
Decide the exact flag values written for each user: dataLimit is stored in MB and 3proxy's d flag takes bytes, expiresAt is a Date and e takes a unix timestamp, ipLimit is already a count. Handle the null cases: an absent dataLimit means unlimited, so no d flag, and the same for expiry. Confirm whether an already-expired user should get e in the past (3proxy refuses them immediately) or be omitted entirely.</description>
<parameter name="details">Read src/lib/proxyauth-writer.ts and src/core/actions/config.ts side by side; both build the same line and must agree. The conversion helpers for MB to bytes and Date to unix seconds already exist in src/app/api/config/generate/route.ts and can be moved rather than rewritten. Careful: dataUsed and dataLimit are BigInt in Prisma, so the conversion goes through Number() first.
subtasks.details:
<info added on 2026-09-26T18:30:33.332Z>
BLOCKING QUESTION ANSWERED by task 14: 3proxy 0.9.5 DOES accept a quoted CR hash inside a users file pulled in by the $ directive. Verified end to end on the real stack, not on a synthetic file. The panel wrote `admin:CR:"$1$..."` through its own updateProxyauthFile, 3proxy was restarted to re-read the file, and then the correct plaintext returned HTTP 200 through the proxy while a wrong password returned 407. So the quoting in proxyauthEntry is correct and the $1$ prefix is understood. Task 8 can proceed on that assumption. Two things still to establish while implementing the flags: whether 3proxy enforces the e expiry flag and the d byte limit in this build, since both can require compile-time support that silently does nothing when absent. Repeat-method note: the sandbox blocks reading or hand-writing the users file, and 3proxy 0.9.5 takes no CLI flags, so the only viable route is to let the application generate the file, restart the 3proxy container, and probe with curl.
</info added on 2026-09-26T18:30:33.332Z>
<info added on 2026-09-26T19:18:02.751Z>
PREMISE INVALIDATED: The d/e/i per-user flags do not exist in 3proxy's user list. Per howtoe.html, USERDESC is exactly three parts (login, password type, password) with only CL, CR, and NT as valid types; access limits are enforced via ACLs, not inline flags. src/conf.c h_users() confirms this mechanically: on a CR entry it takes everything after "CR:" as the password and never parses a fourth field. Measured on the real stack: appending :d1048576 causes 3proxy to treat it as part of the password, resulting in 407 for every user. The repo's code comment claiming "users username:CL:password[:flags]" was incorrect. Limit enforcement must instead come from 3proxy ACL traffic counters (a larger 3proxy.cfg change) or from the panel side, where the fix is that a deactivated user must leave the file entirely, which is now done and verified. This subtask is therefore obsolete and should not be implemented as written.
</info added on 2026-09-26T19:18:02.751Z>

Both writers currently call proxyauthEntry(username, password) and are the only two callers, so changing the signature is contained. Verify the emitted line shape against a real 3proxy, not against the doc example alone. Update tests/unit/core/password-hash.test.ts and tests/unit/core/actions/config.test.ts, which assert on the entry format, and tests/unit/core/actions/config.test.ts currently asserts toContain("activeuser:CR:") which must keep passing.

subtasks.description:
Add one shared guard combining currentSession() with an isAdmin check, and call it as the first statement of every route and action that changes state or returns data. It must fail closed: no valid session, or a session without isAdmin, returns 401 or 403.</description>
<parameter name="details">src/core/session.ts exposes currentSession() returning { isAuthorized, userId, username } but carries no role, so the guard needs a way to know the role. Either widen currentSession to return isAdmin from a database read, which also closes the separate finding that currentSession never re-checks the database, or add a separate helper. Decide once here rather than re-deriving the check in eight routes. Place it next to session.ts. This guard is the fix for the class of bug, not just the eight instances: a route added later should get the check by default.

subtasks.description:
CRITICAL. Close GET /api/config/status and both handlers of /api/config/generate. status/route.ts:12 selects password:true and returns it at :46 with no session check, so one unauthenticated GET dumps every proxy credential. generate/route.ts interpolates the plaintext into the emitted config at :45 and :93. tasks.title: Spike: verify 3proxy accepts quoted CR hashes in a $ included users file
tasks.description:
BLOCKING SPIKE. Determine whether 3proxy 0.9.5 accepts a quoted value `user:CR:"$1$salt$hash"` in a users file pulled in by the `users $file` directive, or whether the quotes become part of the stored hash and break every password. Run a real 3proxy container, write such a file, restart, and attempt authentication with the plaintext.</description>
<parameter name="details">The 3proxy documentation requires quotes around CR values because a leading $ is a file-inclusion macro, but the documented example is an inline `users` command inside 3proxy.cfg, not an entry inside a separate file pulled in by `$`. src/conf.c strips quote characters in parsestr() before the token reaches h_users(), so the hypothesis is that quotes are handled identically in both cases, but this has never been tested. Everything in the enforcement task depends on the answer: if quotes break the hash, the fix is a different mechanism entirely. Method: start 3proxy with a users file containing a quoted $1$ MD5-crypt hash, authenticate over HTTP and SOCKS with the plaintext, and confirm 200 rather than 407. Compare against an unquoted entry. Record the exact file content that works.
tasks.testStrategy: Container run: a quoted $1$ entry authenticates with the plaintext, an unquoted $1$ entry does not, and a wrong plaintext is rejected in both cases. Write down the working file format verbatim so the writer task can copy it.

tasks.title: Remove wildcard CORS headers and bound the log endpoint limit
tasks.description:
Remove Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * from /api/logs (line 54), /api/system/status (line 141) and /api/users/traffic (line 27), and bound the `limit` query parameter on /api/logs. The limit is read as a bare parseInt with no clamp and used as a ceiling while getLogs slurps whole files via readLogFile before slicing, so ?limit=999999999 is a memory and response size DoS.</description>
<parameter name="details">The wildcard CORS header made the log endpoint readable from any website the operator visited, before authentication was added. It is unnecessary even for a same-origin panel and only widens exposure. Bound the limit with a clamp such as Math.min(Math.max(limit ?? 1000, 1), 5000) and reject a non-numeric value instead of letting parseInt produce NaN. Also check readLogFile: it reads the entire file into memory before slicing, so a large log file costs memory regardless of the limit; consider reading only the tail that the limit needs.
tasks.testStrategy: Response headers carry no Access-Control-Allow-Origin. A request with limit=999999999 returns at most the cap. A request with limit=abc does not produce NaN behaviour. Confirm the response size stays bounded for a large log file.

tasks.title: Upgrade Next.js to a release patched against the four middleware-bypass advisories
tasks.description:
Upgrade next from the installed 16.2.3 to a release that closes four open High middleware/proxy-bypass advisories: GHSA-6gpp-xcg3-4w24 (<16.2.11, CVSS 8.3), GHSA-492v-c6pp-mqqv (<16.2.5, dynamic route parameter injection), GHSA-267c-6grr-h53f (<16.2.5, segment prefetch) and GHSA-26hh-7cqf-hhc6 (<16.2.6, incomplete fix). This is a High on its own and is not cosmetic like the headers work it was bundled with in task 13.</description>
<parameter name="details">GHSA-6gpp applies to this project: its condition is Turbopack plus a single locale, Turbopack became the default bundler for next build in 16.0.0, scripts/build.ts runs a bare next build, and there is no i18n config so the single-locale condition holds trivially. Run this as its own change with its own verification, not bundled with config edits, because a Next major or minor bump can move behaviour the build depends on. Check the upgrade guide for the middleware to proxy rename, verify next.config.js still applies, and confirm the Docker build stage still produces a working standalone bundle. Note that the two CRITICAL advisories against next (GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36 Windows path traversal, GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 AVIF RCE) do not apply to a Linux Alpine build, but check that the upgrade does not introduce a new i18n or image-optimizer path that would make the AVIF one reachable.
tasks.testStrategy: npm audit --omit=dev reports no open High or Critical advisory against next. tsc, unit, integration and fail2ban suites pass. The Docker image builds and the standalone bundle serves /api/health. Proxy behaviour (src/proxy.ts) still guards /admin paths.

tasks.title: Verify the fix set end to end and ship a release
tasks.description:
End-to-end verification of the whole fix set, then ship it. Covers: a new E2E test proving a deactivated user is rejected by 3proxy and a user over their data limit is cut off; a container run proving the scheduler reaches its endpoint and .proxyauth carries the flags; an independent security pass re-checking the Critical and High findings are closed and introducing nothing new; and a release. v0.5.1 is already published, so this needs 0.5.2 or later plus a release tag.</description>
<parameter name="details">The enforcement fix is the one that needs proving rather than asserting, because a wrong flag value miscounts a paying customer's traffic. Bring up the real two-container stack, create a user with a small data limit, drive traffic through 3proxy until the limit is exceeded, restart 3proxy and confirm the user is refused. Then deactivate a user outright and confirm authentication fails after a restart. Only after both pass, run the independent security pass. This is also the point to settle whether docker-compose.yml stays gitignored now that it no longer contains a hardcoded secret, which is a decision the owner should make explicitly rather than by omission.
tasks.testStrategy: Two new E2E assertions: a deactivated user receives an auth failure from 3proxy, and a user past their data limit is cut off. Container run shows .proxyauth with flags and the scheduler succeeding. Independent audit reports no open Critical or High. Release tag published and the multi-arch image carries both platforms.

tasks.title: Decide whether to pursue native 3proxy traffic limiting via ACL counters
tasks.description:
OPTIONAL / DECISION REQUIRED. Native per-user traffic limiting is now the only remaining enforcement gap, and it is not reachable from the users file. 3proxy defines a user entry as exactly login:type:password with CL, CR and NT as the only types, and directs limits to ACLs; its auth.c enforces limits from conf.trafcounter, which is populated from 3proxy.cfg rather than from the users list. Work out what that requires in this deployment and decide whether it is worth doing, because panel-side enforcement now actually works: a user who exceeds their quota is set inactive and leaves the file, so 3proxy refuses them on the next reload.</description>
<parameter name="details">Tradeoff to weigh. Panel-side enforcement depends on the panel being up and on a maintenance run happening, so a user can overshoot by whatever they transfer between runs, and enforcement stops entirely if the panel is down. Native enforcement would cut off inside 3proxy and keep working when the panel is not, but it means generating and managing per-user ACL rules in 3proxy.cfg, which the panel does not currently write at all, and it may need compile-time support in the 3proxy build that silently does nothing when absent. First step is to establish whether the shipped 3proxy/3proxy:0.9.5 image supports per-user traffic counters at all, and what the config syntax is; the howtoe ACL section covers allow, deny and flush but the counter directive was not located in the documentation read so far. Not blocking: the deactivated-user fix in task 9 removed the silent failure, so limits are enforced as of that commit, just not natively.
tasks.testStrategy: Spike: determine the counter directive and whether the shipped build honours it, by configuring a limit for one user in 3proxy.cfg and pushing traffic past it. If the build lacks support, record that and close the task as not applicable.

tasks.title: Keep the traffic sync offsets on the data volume, not in the image layer
tasks.description:
SYNC_INFO_FILE defaults to path.join(process.cwd(), "data", "traffic-sync.json"), and in the container cwd is /app/.next/standalone, so the per-inode log offsets land at /app/.next/standalone/data/traffic-sync.json, inside the image layer rather than on the /app/data volume. The file is lost whenever the container is recreated from the image, the offsets reset to zero, and every logged byte is accounted again. Point SYNC_INFO_FILE at /app/data in the compose stacks, or derive it from the database location so it follows the volume automatically. Found while verifying the maintenance scheduler: the job reported success and regenerated the user file, but no traffic-sync.json existed under /app/data. The impact is double counting rather than an outage, which for a metered service means billing twice for the same traffic. The integration test sets SYNC_INFO_FILE explicitly, which is why the suite never caught it. The same class of problem applies to any other default path that resolves against cwd rather than the volume.</description>
<parameter name="file">.taskmaster/tasks/tasks.json
tasks.testStrategy: Container run: after a maintenance pass the offsets file exists under /app/data, and after recreating the container a second pass reports zero newly accounted bytes instead of re-reading the whole log.
